speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 75, respecting fair wages and hours of labour in relation to public works and contracts.
He said: On behalf of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), who is absent, I beg to introduce this bill. I may explain that the bill will operate as a repeal of the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act of 1930, and in addition to re-ena'oting many of the clauses of that act it will provide new sections to comply as far as possible with the recommendations of the price spreads commission. It makes provision for an eight hour day and a forty-four hour week upon government works and contracts, and it extends the federal government's policy of fair wages and the forty-four hour week to works and contracts towards which federal aid is granted by way of contribution, subsidy, loan, advance or guarantee, by providing that in all contracts hereafter entered into conditions shall be imposed which shall bind the contractors to maintain the same standard of hours and wages. These are the only changes in the bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 48, to amend and consolidate the acts relating to patents of invention.

Before second reading carries I want to say a few words. I might perhaps have avoided

Patents of Invention-Mr. Itinjret
doing it, as I was going to suggest that the discussion should take place when the bill is in committee. This bill was introduced in the Senate and received full consideration in the higher chamber. It was also before a special committee there, several witnesses were heard, and I think the bill comes to us in pretty good shape generally. I take this occasion to commend the practice by any government of introducing bills of this nature in the higher chamber, where work is less congested, because when such a measure comes to us a certain amount of consideration has been given to it, and that is for the good of both chambers. I may say further that the Patent Act is one which is always under consideration by a certain portion of the public, many amendments are sought from the department and the minister every year. When I was in charge of that department, on several occasions associations as well as individuals came to the department to secure extensive amendments to the act or to suggesting consolidation. Therefore if any principle is involved in this second reading, reserving any opinion as to the different sections of the bill, I favour this consolidation, with the hope that when adopted the measure may stand for several years without requiring further change. I think it might have been an advantage for this house to have had this bill considered in a special committee, but everyone will understand that at this late stage of the session that would not be feasible. In the hope that the house may be able to dispose of this measure in an expeditious way in committee of the whole I will not say anything further at present. I think we can well deal with the questions as they arise from section to section.

I do not rise in any spirit of criticism of this bill, but there is a matter which I understand is not dealt with in it, and as there would be no clause under which the matter could be brought up in the committee stage as far as I know, I would like to lay before the government one phase in connection with patents which I trust might be considered when the bill is before the committee. I refer to the practice of concerns in Canada, and I think the same practice is followed in other countries, of taking advantage of the Patent Act for the enhancement of the price of goods, to a degree perhaps unwarranted in the circumstances. I may illustrate the point by incidents which came to my attention some months ago and which were brought to the attention of the official in charge of the act at that time. These had to do with electric light bulbs. I want it clearly understood that I am not
bringing this matter forward at the present time merely to mention this incident, but it illustrates the point to which I wish to refer.
Electric light bulbs are manufactured in Canada under patents held by certain companies. They are sold, in the case of a one hundred watt bulb, at around 55 or 60 cents each. Dealers in this class of goods assert that they can buy the same general type of bulbs which have paid all the patent royalties and observed all the provisions of the law in the United States or in Holland, pay a duty of some thirty or forty per cent and sell them in Canada at from twenty-eight to thirty-five cents retail. I should complete the statement by saying that after observing the patent laws of the country where they were produced and paying the duty charged by the Canadian customs authorities and so on, when they sought to enter these bulbs through the customs, after an appeal to certain sections of the Patent Act, they were not permitted to import them into Canada because the patent rights in this country had been reserved.
The point at issue there is simply this: Under the international agreement regarding patents and trade marks, if a certain article has been manufactured in a foreign country, with all the provisions of the patent law of that country being observed, it ought not to be an offence to bring that article into Canada providing a reasonable protection is given through customs duties if that happens to be the government policy at the time. Having observed all the regulations in the country of manufacture and having paid the duty I submit it ought to be possible to import those articles into Canada. Under the law as it now stands, however, that cannot be done and in this particular instance the Patent Act serves really as a duty of about eighty per cent in addition to the twenty-five or thirty-five per cent charged under the customs laws.
My submission is that the Patent Act never should be used or permitted to be used as a supplementary customs duty or protection. I think that should be made clear. I should like to state also that in drawing this matter to the attention of parliament I only do so because now the act is in a major state of revision before the house. I am not criticising any government, past or present, in regard to the matter; I am bringing to the attention of the house a situation that has developed and been disclosed, so far as I am concerned, only during the past year. I have a good deal of information on the matter before me, and I should like to read briefly from a reference with regard to an investigation made by the federal trade commission of the United States, who in 1928 conducted an inquiry into the

Patents oj Invention-Mr. Stevens
question of electrical equipment and competitive conditions of the electric power industry. They found the electrical industry to be dominated if not controlled by an international group of electrical manufacturers, each member of which is the most powerful in its respective community. The members of this international organization exchange .patent rights, manufacturing processes and other trade secrets. This exchange is characterized by a division of territory, and I should like to direct particular attention to this:
This exchange is characterized by a division of territory, each company granting to the other exclusive rights in specified countries, described as exclusive territory; or nonexclusive rights in other countries described as non-exclusive territory, and reserving all rights in still other countries described as excluded territory. Such agreements practically eliminate any competition of a serious nature. For example, in the case of light bulbs, in so far as Canada is concerned no independent manufacturer can either manufacture or sell in Canada without being liable for suit for lrnringement of patents which are owned by the larger organization-represented in Canada by the Canadian General Electric Company Limited, and Canadian Westinghouse Company Limited. These two firms as members of the international group have been "given" a Canadian market, and by the mere threat of suit are usually successful in disposing of any likely competitor.
That statement was made in 1928 by the federal trade commission of the United States, so I am told, but the facts are slightly different to-day. I understand, though I am speaking subject to correction, that there are now five companies in Canada, but the other companies have been added only by licence of the older or larger companies, and all these are represented by one concern. When certain dealers brought in or attempted to bring in bulbs from foreign countries, in one case Holland and in two or three other cases the United States, this one concern brought suit against the importers, secured injunctions and subjected them to a great deal of loss and inconvenience.
I would have no criticism of these companies in protecting their patent rights in Canada providing they sold their goods to the public at a reasonable and fair rate. I am quite aware of the answer that may be made; I have not had time to look up the section of the act but I am quite aware that it does provide that the commissioner of patents, I believe under the instructions of the minister, may interfere, and I think he has power actually to fix prices where he has reason to believe that abuses have occurred. In practice however, this does not happen; as a matter of practice I doubt if there is any great interference.

There is another feature which I think ought to be taken into consideration in dealing with this matter. I had under my hand, and I sent forward to the proper official in the proper department, a long list of patents affecting these articles held by these companies; if I remember correctly the list included several hundred patents, or we will say in the neighbourhood of over one hundred; the exact number I have not in mind or under my hand. The question arises as to how many of these patents, frequently bought up and controlled by the larger corporations, are ever put into actual operation. Here again I quite admit that there is an answer. The answer is that if they are not put into operation within eighteen months or some certain limited period of time the commissioner may declare them open, but again that does not work in practice. The situation is quite obvious. A man perfects an invention and, if it is good, immediately it is sought after and secured if possible by one of the large corporations. They are strong and wealthy, if the new invention affects some invention they are already manufacturing in large quantities they can easily afford to pay a very large sum, comparatively speaking, for the invention. The individual is satisfied; he is paid off, and the patent now belongs to the large corporation. It is pigeon-holed and the chances are that no one in the country has any knowledge of it, except those in the patent office, but the patent commissioner is not there for the purpose of checking up to see whether or not patents are used. Unless someone brings the matter to the attention of the patent commissioner there is little likelihood of any action being taken. Here again I submit that in this general revision the act ought to be so changed that where patents have been issued some body, some official or some official body should be clothed with the authority, to follow up those patents to see whether or not they are used, and if they are not used for the benefit of the general public some explanation ought to be forthcoming as to why they are not used. I am convinced from quite a lot of thought and investigation I carried on in connection with the subject some six or eight months ago that there is a large number of patents particularly electrical patents and others in other lines of industry resting in the archives of many corporations which would be useful to the public, which ought to be put into operation and use, but which are not used because they conflict with some general and practical object now being manufactured in large quantities.

May I ask a question?

Patents of Invention

Mr. Stevens
Yes.
I should like to ask the hon. -member if the difficulty might not be solved by giving newspaper notoriety to patents after the time has expired within *which they are protected.

That is quite true, but it is not the point about which I am speaking. I am refering to patents which have not been used either before or after the expiry date. There is no doulbt about it however that publicity would do much to cure the difficulty, and I shall have a suggestion to make in that respect.
In the price spreads report reference has been made to placing the administration of the commercial side of the Patent Act-not necessarily the legal side, because there are -two sides, legal and commercial

under a body such as is recommended, namely the -trade and industry commission. In any case there ought to be an official body of some kind or a business department responsible for the administration of the commercial side of the patent law, so that they could keep track of and check on- patents which have been issued, ascertain to what extent they are being used or pigeon-holed as the case may be, or to what extent the holders of a patent right are abusing that privilege in the manner I have mentioned, namely, by virtually turning it into a secon-dary customs protection.
These are two matters to which I should like to draw the attention of the house, and I feel that unless it is done in this revision there is not much hope of having any remedial action taken for a great many years. It is true that the commissioner of patents may order the patentee- to supply the patented article within reasonable limits at such price as may be fixed by him and in accordance with the trade. It may be answered this afternoon that that provision in the act takes care of the situation. I submit that in the first place the practice demonstrates it is not done and in the second- place I submit that under the present method of administration of the act the patent commissioner is so engrossed with his other duties and with, shall I say, the vision of his duties which has grown up through the years that this feature of it is practically ignored or neglected, not with intent but simply as a matter of form and practice.
That is why I suggest that the matter should be considered seriously because I am convinced of this, namely, that in this one instance alone, the manufacture and sale in Canada of electric -light bulbs, the public
are paying a price which I would say is at *least 30 per cent or 40 per cent above that which they ought to pay for this class of goods. If it is true in this instance it may be true in a great many other instances. As a matter of fact I have not any doubt that it is true in other instances and therefore I suggest that -before this measure leaves the committee stage of the house some provision should -be made for an adequate protection of the consumer in regard to this matter. I again suggest to the government that they consider the placing of the administration of the commercial features of the act under some business organization or body, official or board whose duty it shall be to check on these commercial sides or features of the patent laws of the country.
Mr. Speaker, this bill-
Will the minister not close the debate if he speaks?
I have not opened it yet; I have not had the opportunity.
He opened it when he seconded the motion.

I rise to a point of order. Does not the minister on the actual motion open the debate, and therefore is he not out of order in speaking at this time unless it is agreed that by his speech he closes the debate? He has already spoken.

I have no objection to the point of order standing. When the bill was called I rose in my place to make a preliminary introduction, but another hon. member caught the eye of the Speaker and proceeded. I suggest however that this debate on the details of the bill might better take place when we are discussing the separate sections.

I do not wish to interrupt the minister nor do I raise a point of order, but I am simply trying to protect my right to speak. So far as I am personally concerned I should be very glad to have the minister make any statement in connection with the bill which he desires to make. Certainly I do not wish to interfere with that right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Go ahead.
Yes, go on.

Mr. Speaker, I am much impressed by the number of persons who have come to me during the last two or three years with representations regarding patents, and when the patent measure was introduced by the minister I wrote him and suggested that it would be in the best interests of the House of Commons

Patents of Invention-Mr. Coote
and all people concerned if the bill were sent to a select or special committee of this chamber. However that was not done. This measure was sent to the Senate, and I believe it has been considered by a committee of that chamber. There are one or two points however which I should like to bring to the attention of the house before the bill receives second reading.
I have been much impressed by the statements made by the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) who has just taken his seat. I should like to impress upon the house that the people generally have an interest in most patents granted to-day. A great many patents, and particularly in industries such as the electrical industry, are the result of work of scientists and engineers employed by the electrical companies. Practically all of these men have received their training or education in some university which is at least in part kept up by the state. When these men secure employment in large corporations I believe they must sign agreements to the effect that the benefits of any inventions or discoveries they may make must go to the corporations employing them. If these men have been educated at least in part at the expense of the public it does not seem fair that the results of their discoveries should benefit commercial enterprises, or that the benefits arising from their discoveries should go to corporations. The public have an interest in all inventions which arise as a result of their labours. I believe the best way to deal with the matter would be to set up a board with power to determine the royalty which would be paid for the use of any patent, and to decide to whom the royalties should be paid'-whether to some corporation, an individual or to be divided and allow anyone to manufacture the article on payment of royalty. I have been convinced by representations made to me at different times that the public are paying a tremendous price for some of the patented articles that are in common use throughout the country and that the Patent Act is one of the corner stones of monopoly in Canada. About a year ago I had brought to my attention a certain type of grain cleaner used in western' Canada. In many instances this apparatus is installed on grain separators, the grain going through it as it comes through the threshing machine. The cost of the cleaner installed on the grain separator ranges from $420 to $460. I never heard of it being sold for less than $420. The implement agent in Calgary who told me about this said that he had taken the trouble to inquire what it would cost to have one of

these machines manufactured and installed on the separator, and he assured me that if it were not for the patent right interfering, this machine could be made and placed on the separator at a price which would enable him to sell it to the farmer at approximately $200. Let us assume that a royalty of $20 was paid to the inventor of that grain separator, and surely that would be considered sufficient for him. Then the invention would be available to the farmers at a cost of approximately $220, which is about fifty per cent of the price we are forced to pay to-day. It may be possible to overcome some of these things through administration by the methods suggested by the hon. member for East Kootenay, but it is the duty of this house I think to see that if possible some change is made in the act itself or in its administration so that these things will be available to the people at a price which we can afford to pay and which will also allow ample remuneration to the inventor himself.
As I said a moment ago the present Patent Act is one of the cornerstones of monopoly, and I think we are all agreed here that monopoly makes possible tremendous over-capitalization. Monopoly deprives the people of the beneficial effects of many inventions. Radio is an outstanding example. It would seem to me that any future invention for the improvement of radio would be useless to anybody except those who hold the patents under which the present radios have been built. So any inventor who perfects some improved process in regard to radio and patents it, is at the mercy of the radio holding trust. I do not know whether I am giving it the right name, but I am told that there is a holding company which holds these patents for the large corporations. If we were to change the act in the manner I have suggested so that anyone who was willing to pay a royalty to be determined by a government board might make use of any invention, I think that would go a long way towards decentralizing some of the big monopolies, and the decentralization of industry is something that is so desirable to-day.
I do hope that before the act is allowed to receive its third reading careful consideration will be given to the proposal which I have made to set up a board to fix a royalty on patents, after which any person who is willing to pay that royalty may make use of the patent. That would allow the public to get the benefit of many of these inventions which to-day are possibly being withheld from us, either actually withheld through misuse,

Patents of Invention-Mr. Bothwell
or withheld because of the exorbitant price which is asked for them. There are one or two other objectionable features of the present Patent Act which I think ought to be changed, but I have emphasized the point which I think should be stressed at this moment on the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker,. I have just one word to add to the question which I asked the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens). It does seem to me that a lot of our difficulties in connection with patents granted could be overcome if something in the nature of a publication were got out by the commissioner of patents showing when the time for manufacturing a patented article in Canada had expired. It has been generally stated that patents are pigeonholed, and as has been explained by the hon. member for East Kootenay, nobody has any particular knowledge of these patents. But if the commissioner of patents were compelled to give public notification either in the Canada Gazette or some other publication of the patents that had been granted and had not been made use of, it seems to me that a lot of the difficulty would be solved without the necessity of setting up any board.
There is also the other question of patents being held and being made use of to build up a monopolistic trade. I am not so sure that that could not also be overcome through the commissioner of patents by publication, and without the necessity of creating any extra board or setting up any committee or some business organization or body, giving the public an idea of what patents are in existence and which they may find an opportunity of making use of. Then the opportunity for competition will be given.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this patent bill was introduced by me to this house in January of this year, and I then made some explanation of the nature and purpose of the amendments suggested in the bill. It really was one advance step in the matter of legislation relating to the Department of the Secretary of State. In August, 1930, when I assumed that office I found in the administration of that department that its effective operation was restricted somewhat by the legislation then in force, and experience from week to week and month to month suggested to me certain amendments.
In the session of 1931 I introduced amendments to the Copyright Amendment Act to comply with the obligations that Canada had
assumed under the Rome convention of 1928 to which Canada had adhered, and to provide for effective means of investigating and restricting the royalties, fees and charges of those companies and associations which controlled performing rights in music. In the same session I introduced to this house an act to amend the Naturalization Act, to protect Canadian women who married aliens and who did not thereby acquire the nationality of their husbands. That act as passed by this house was subsequently accepted by the imperial parliament, which made amendments to its own naturalization act in conformity with the amendments made by this parliament.
In the session of 1932 I prepared and submitted to this parliament bills to amend the Boards of Trade Act and also to amend the Patent Act; a bill respecting the civil service of Canada, and a very important bill indeed entitled An Act Respecting Unfair Competition in Trade and Commerce, which was to carry into effect a certain convention which had been entered into at The Hague by the previous government, and with respect to which that government had not, previous to going out of office owing to dissolution of parliament, been able to promote confirmatory legislation.
In the session of 1933 I prepared and introduced a very important bill, An Act to facilitate compromises and arrangements between companies and their creditors, the validity of which was questioned by one or more of the provinces, but which was subsequently upheld by the unanimous decision of the Supreme Court of Canada.
In 1934 I prepared and submitted to this house three very important measures relating to the Department of the Secretary of State: one, an act to amend the Oaths of Allegiance Act, which passed this house unanimously, although similar legislation was the subject of very acrimonious debate in two of our sister dominions; also an act to provide for a Bureau of Translations, with respect to which there were differences of opinion in this house; and also an act respecting dominion companies, which involved the redrafting of dominion company legislation to give better protection to the public and to insure the more prudent administration of the business affairs of these companies. And then came this last measure dealing with patents. In order to secure an improvement in the legislation with regard to patents, in the early years of this administration I asked a certain committee to organize and sit under the chairmanship of the senior judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, and that committee advanced very admirable sug-



Patents of Invention-Mr. Cahan
gestions. It was however unable to come to an agreement as to whether in the improvements in our patent law we should follow the American legislation or should follow what many believed to be the best patent legislation existing, that is, the patent act of the United Kingdom.
In this bill many of the difficulties which arose in the administration of the Patent Act now in existence have I think been entirely overcome. It is true, as suggested by the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens), that the establishment of a patent monopoly in Canada by any patentee has hitherto enabled that patentee to maintain his monopoly, although reasonable efforts were not made for the effective working of the patent in Canada, that is, for the effective manufacture and sale in Canada at reasonable prices of the patented article. I found in the administration of that act, as suggested, that a foreign patentee who, under the international convention to which we are parties, has a right to apply within one year for a patent in Canada, has frequently obtained the patent in Canada without proceeding to the effective manufacture here under that patent, but he has in times past appointed an agent in Canada whose chief duty it was to conserve the monopoly rights in Canada of the foreign patentee, with the result that, although manufacture was not undertaken in Canada, the agent in Canada of such patentee was able to keep fully advised as to the importations of articles which infringed the Canadian monopoly and by exacting payment of a royalty in Canada, which was not regulated, was enabled to maintain in Canada very high prices for the articles manufactured abroad by the foreign patentee.
When this bill was introduced it contained some very stringent proposals to overcome these difficulties. Owing to the press of work here and the lack of legislative work in another branch of parliament, the bill was dropped here and introduced in the Senate. It was then brought before the Senate committee on banking and commerce. I attended that committee in order to watch its proceedings from day to day and week to week, and I do not think that in recent years in parliament any committee has ever shown the same active interest in a bill as was shown by that committee of the Senate. Day after day and week after week witnesses from all parts of Canada appeared before that committee and gave evidence with regard to the alleged evils which bad arisen by reason of the lack of certain improvements which were proposed in the bill. Finally, after several weeks, the bill
[Mr. Cahao.3
passed the committee of the Senate and the Senate, and is now before this house for second reading.
I do not intend at this stage to enter upon a discussion of particular sections of the bill. One difficulty I found in the administration of the act was that, except by the appointment of a royal commission under the Inquiries Act, there was no way by which the Secretary of State, or the patent commissioner, who was acting as the head of this branch of the Department of the Secretary of State, could ascertain definitely whether a certain patent was really being actively worked in Canada, that is, that the patented articles were being manufactured in Canada and sold at reasonable prices and under reasonable conditions. The result was that we introduced a new section which is found in this bill, that is, section 64, whereby the commissioner may at any time apply to any patentee for a return showing whether the patented invention is being worked on a commercial scale in Canada, the place where worked, the name and address of the person by whom the patent is being so worked, and the reasons, if any, why such patented invention is not being worked in Canada. And the failure to make complete answer to such a request is an admission by the patentee that the patented invention is not being worked. But that was not deemed quite sufficient, and so we proceeded with section 65, which is an entirely new section; and we there provided for certain compulsory licences in case of abuse, and also section 66, which is entirely new to our legislation, and which is a verbal reproduction of the English act, has been incorporated in this bill. And under these provisions I suggest that the evils, at least so far as they can be controlled by legislation, are being controlled in this act. I think an opportunity should be given to the department to ascertain whether it may not be effectively administered so as to obviate the evils which have been mentioned and some of which undoubtedly exist. I say personally, having been in that office now for five years, that so far as effective administration goes, an effective administration has been given under the several statutes then in force, and so far as an intelligent effort could be made to introduce remedial measures, to make the administration of the several acts more effective, those remedial measures have, as I have already suggested, been brought before the house.	_
This measure is I think the culmination of such efforts as I have been able to make to secure satisfactory legislation under which that branch of the department of the department of the Secretary of State could be effectively

Patents of Invention
administered. I believe this legislation, if enacted, will remedy the objections which some hon. gentlemen have made, and I trust the house in its wisdom will adopt this bill in almost its entirety so as to see if it can be so administered as to maintain intact our obligations under the international conventions to which we are parties, so as to preserve intact the reasonable rights of patentees, and so as to conserve effectively the public interest as to both the production or manufacture in Canada and the sale at reasonable prices in Canada of the patented article. I can assure the house that neither this nor any other measure which I have introduced has been introduced with any partisan purpose whatever. I have endeavoured to give the subject the most intelligent consideration that was possible for me, and also to give in the meantime as effective an administration of existing acts as it was possible to give.

On section 40-Chemical products and substances.

I shall now make an explanation of the point raised by the hon. member. In the second line of section 40 the word "and" now appears. An amendment substituting "and" for "or" was made some years ago when the Patent Act was before this house for revision. Its significance is that when the war broke out the British government found that certain chemical products were controlled under German inventions, and that the disclosures made at the time the applications for patents were pending at the British patent office were not sufficient to enable the British government, after the patents were forfeited, to manufacture or produce the same substance. Under the method which had prevailed prior to that date if an applicant received a patent for a chemical process the patent included the product produced by that process. The British authorities did not agree to continue that provision of their law, namely that the patenting of a process would ipso facto confer a patent for the substance produced by the process. This parliament decided otherwise at a previous revision. Now if a patent of a process is obtained in Canada, then that patent extends and applies to the product produced by that process. That does not obtain in England, but I believe in other countries the patent applies to the product.
After a discussion lasting one or two days the committee of the Senate decided that as parliament knowingly and wittingly had come
Patents of Invention
to a decision in 1918 to that effect, and as that provision had been continued and maintained throughout the subsequent years it was inadvisable to make an innovation in our law with respect to it. So that if a patent is secured by a process over a certain substance thereby produced, then in Canada the product is also patented unless it is otherwise produced, and the assumption is that when it is produced it is produced by the patented process unless the contrary be absolutely shown in the courts.
I would ask the Secretary of State if it has been found that many countries do not recognize the patent laws.

I think all the leading
countries of the world are now parties to the same convention to which we are a party. I could easily look up the list. There are four pages of signatories to this convention.

Do they live up to the
spirit of the agreement?

I think they try to. We
have had no complaints whatever during the last five years from Canadian patentees, that is, from patentees resident in Canada, that on applying to foreign patent offices they have not received their just rights under the terms of the outstanding convention. Complaint has not been made in five years.

Would the one receiving the (patent have the control of that product irrespective of the fact that the product might have been produced by different methods prior to the granting of that patent?

Under our law as it has stood for some eighteen years it is assumed that if the product produced is identical, then that it is produced by the patented process which produces that substance. I see what is in the hon. gentleman's mind. We fought that out for days, but we have decided to maintain the law as it is, and any arguments to the contrary did not prevail.

With further reference to that matter, Mr. Chairman, even if a company has received a patent for a certain process of manufacturing a certain drug or chemical, in the event of this drug or chemical being produced by other processes it does

appear to me to be ridiculous merely because of the fact that this company gets a patent for a new process of producing this commodity, that it should be given patent rights over the whole commodity. That seems ridiculous to me.

That is an assumption which is created by statute, and the final judgment of the Senate committee was that that was a fair assumption under the circumstances. Of course, that assumption may be rebutted by positive evidence.

On section 45-What patent shall contain and confer.
Would the Secretary of State kindly give us an interpretation of this section?

The section reads:
Every patent granted under this act shall contain the title or name of the invention, with a reference to the specification, and shall, subject to the conditions in this act prescribed, grant to the patentee and his legal representatives for the term therein mentioned, from the granting of the same, the exclusive right, privilege and liberty of making, constructing, using and vending to others to be used the said invention, subject to adjudication in respect thereof before any court of competent jurisdiction.
The only new provision there is the words underlined, "in this act prescribed." This section has been the basis of the patent law of Canada for all time. The only change is that we have introduced entirely new conditions with respect to the manufacture and sale, and the price at which the article is sold, and therefore to make it clear that the grant of the patent would confer no overriding rights the words were introduced "subject to the conditions in this act prescribed," so that the conditions subsequently stated and prescribed in the act will apply notwithstanding the terms at which the patent is granted.
Is there anywhere in this act a limit put on the special profits that can be charged on account of the patent?
Who decides what reasonable terms are?

There is a long provision [DOT]which we shall reach in a few moments in regard to the patent. The commissioner may [DOT]make full inquiry, at the instance of any

party, and may make a finding, but that finding is subject to appeal to an exchequer court judge. So that the exchequer court judge has the final adjudication in the matter.

Section 45, which we are now discussing, makes it possible for certain corporations to obtain an absolute monopoly of certain things which are in general use in Canada. It grants "the exclusive right, privilege and liberty of making, constructing, using and vending to others," and so on. Nothing has been left out which would grant them the very widest and most exclusive rights of every kind. I should be very much obliged if the Secretary of State would explain why it is advisable or necessary to give any patentee the exclusive right of vending to others any invention. Surely when he has the exclusive right of making, constructing and using any invention the right to vend it might be left open. It may be that there is some good reason for putting in this provision, but I have never yet been able to understand why any patentee should be given the exclusive right of vending to others. If he can set the price on the article that ought to be enough.

A patent is a monopoly and it is in the terms a complete monopoly; it always has been a monopoly since the days that patents were first granted by the crown or by any governmental authority. It is a monopoly and a subsisting monopoly, and one which by international convention we are bound to maintain within certain limits prescribed by the convention. What we have done in section 45 is to grant a monopoly, but we grant it subject to the conditions in this act prescribed; and in the subsequent sections we have gone as far as any act in existence of which I know, or to which I can gain access and prescribed conditions which would relieve such monopoly of its most prejudicial features. I have gone as far as I can.

For my part I object to section 45. Possibly when we have seen the conditions to which the minister refers and which appear in subsequent sections we shall find this section less objectionable; it may be that I shall be convinced then that the section is all right. At the moment, however, I am very much opposed to giving this exclusive right. The right to vend is particularly objectionable. I do not see why we should use all the powers of the state to grant such a monopoly. We are extending a great privilege to any inventor when we
Patents of Invention
patent his invention and safeguard it so that he gets a reasonable reward for his work and we prevent anyone from robbing him of the benefits of the invention. But to grant him the exclusive right to vend it to the general public is objectionable. Are we required by the international convention to put in these words or words to this effect in our Patent Act?

Undoubtedly we are. If parliament decides at some time or other to give a year's notice and withdraw from the convention, that is a matter for discussion and decision, and such a decision would be very farreaching. I may assure the hon. gentleman, however, that having granted the patent, as prescribed by this section,-and the section is no more farreaching than the Patent Act of the United States or of Great Britain or of France-then we have gone as far as we may under the convention in prescribing the working conditions for the purpose of rendering the monopoly as-
As innocuous as possible.
-as prejudicially inoperative as possible.

Seeing that this is the really important section, or one of the most important sections, will the minister say that the subsequent sections containing the conditions under which the patent may be granted will take care of the situation outlined this afternoon by the hon. member for East Kootenay on the second reading?

I understood the statements of the hon. member for East Kootenay to refer to abuses which had arisen with respect to the existing Patent Act, and of those abuses I am fully advised; I have been aware of some of them for five years. We have gone as far as we can, in drafting this bill, to provide ways and means of obviating these abuses and we have prescribed remedial measures. I found no lack of disposition on the part of the Senate committee to deal with such abuses, but we took the very best legal advice available and decided that we really could not effectively go further than the British parliament had done in prescribing remedies for the same abuses. It will be noted that the complaint is that they have been handling lamps of United States manufacture, and the second point is that they have been merchandising lamps, not manufacturing, not infringing on the rights of others, but simply merchandising or selling. Their third assertion is that this is an infringement of the letters patent. I direct the attention of the committee to the extract I read from the investigation of the federal trade commission of the United States. I intend to repeat only part of it. It will be noted that this investigation has this to say:
The members of this international organization exchange patent rights, manufacturing .processes and other "trade secrets." TMb exchange is characterized by a division of territory, each company granting to the other exclusive rights in specified countries.
I ask the committee particularly to notice those words. Further it says:
Such agreements practically eliminate any competition of a serious nature. For example, in the case of light bulbs, in so far as Canada is concerned no independent manufacturer can either manufacture or sell in Canada without being liable for suit for infringement of patents which are owned by the larger organization.
My submission in the first place is that the contention of this firm of solicitors, acting for the Canadian General Electric incandescent lamp patent, is really based upon this international agreement rather than any bona fide infringement of the law, as I shall try to show in a moment. In other words, this company in conjunction with the General Electric in the United States and the other companies that form this international cartel have farmed out the territory of the world, Canada being farmed out to these four firms I have mentioned, and any one who impinges upon the limitation of territory decided by the cartel is penalized by our courts through the Patent Act. The pbwers of the Patent Act that they invoke are, I submit, very narrow. As I read the correspondence and dealt with some of these cases when I was in the Department of Trade and Commerce I was amazed to find the extent-I do not want to be offensive;

Patents of Invention
I almost said the audacity-to which these Canadian firms used the law for their own purposes. I am not speaking now, shall I say, in any privileged place, because I had a talk with the general manager of the Canadian General Electric Company who in my presence frankly took the position that he was quite entitled to all the advantages of the law that he might desire. I put to him the point I raised here; I said, " For the moment I am not concerned with the infringement of patents from a bona fide standpoint. What I am concerned with is your use of the patent law to obtain an additional one hundred per cent protection." That is the point with which I am concerned, and he was unable to show me that his prices were not as I have indicated, namely, sixty cents for a given article with a discount of five cents to certain buyers, and therefore fifty-five cents to some, whereas a similar article after having discharged all the obligations under the patent laws of the United States-to the same company, by the way, and its affiliates-with regard to royalty and so forth, having strictly observed the law and having paid the Canadian customs duty, could be sold in this country for twenty-six cents.
It is obvious that in Canada the companies are taking advantage of, first, the agreement parcelling out the territory and then of the patent law in order to make those agreements good, thus penalizing the importer. There was the case of a gentleman in Ottawa named Feldberg. A judgment was obtained against him without his knowledge; his solicitor, the late Moses Doctor, died!; a judgment was obtained) against him for some S160, I think, and he was precluded from dealing in these articles. There was also a firm down in New Brunswick who took up the matter with me and with others; they were faced with the proceedings I have mentioned here.
For the moment the point I wish to emphasize is this:	powerful institutions
possessed of, and capable of possessing themselves still further of, certain inventions are thus able to preclude what might be called a reasonable traffic in these things, and to maintain an unwarranted price. The minister says these matters are adequately dealt with in sections 64 and 65 of the bill. I invite the committee to follow me for a moment; I will try to make my statement clear and not too lengthy. It will be seen that section 64 takes the place of section 40 of the old act, and I should like to indicate what the old act contained and how it provided for this situation. I will admit that the provision was not put into operation and
therefore was not made effective, but there were certain powers contained in section 40 of the old act, as follows:
Every patent, except those governed' by the provisions of this act relating to the granting of patents to persons in the public service, shall be subject to the following conditions:-
Then it goes on:
(b) Any person interested may present a petition to the commissioner alleging that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to a patent invention have not been satisfied or that the patentee has failed to manufacture adequately the patented invention in Canada, and praying that the patentee be ordered to supply the patented article at a reasonable price or grant licences for the use of the invention on reasonable terms.
Note those words. Then the commissioner shall consider the petition, and the section continues:
-shall proceed to hear and determine the matter, and if it is proved to his satisfaction that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied or that the patentee has failed to adequately manufacture the patented' invention in Canada, the patentee may be ordered by him-
Note these words:
-to supply the patented article within reasonable limits at such price as may be fixed by him and in accordance with the custom of the trade-
I quote further:
-or to grant licences for the use of the patented invention as may be fixed by him-
Later it provides:
-the commissioner may, with the approval of the minister, instead of hearing and determining the matter himself, refer the petition to the exchequer court, which shall have jurisdiction in the premises and may make such order thereon as the commissioner is authorized to make under this section.
I pause to direct attention to this: Under that old section the commissioner did have certain powers. I state very frankly that I do not think they were used very extensively, but if it were found that there was an abuse by a patentee with regard to price he had power to order the supply of the patented invention within reasonable limits at such price as might be fixed by him, and further it might be taken to the exchequer court. Unless I am corrected in this-and I welcome correction if I am wrong-the question of the exchequer court is excluded from the new sections. I shall now read section 64, and although I shall not attempt to read the whole of it I shall read so as to get the sense of it.
The commissioner may ... require the patentee ... to transmit and' deliver to the

(a)	whether the patented invention is being worked on a commercial scale in Canada, and the place where the name and address of the person by whom the patented invention is being so worked; and

And so on. That is substituted for the clause to which I previously referred. It will be, noted that section 64 does not meet the case in anything like the degree that the deleted section 40 of the old act did.
I now come to section 65, to which considerable reference has been made this afternoon. Section 65 reads in part as follows-and I would ask the committee to note it carefully as I proceed:
The attorney general of Canada or any person interested may at any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the grant of a patent apply to the commissioner alleging in the case of that patent that there has been an abuse of the exclusive rights thereunder and asking for relief under this act.
I pause there. In the first place it will be noted that such application can be made only after three years. It may be argued that that is not unreasonable, but I ask, Mr. Chairman: Why the limitation of three years? I want the committee to note this point-and this is known by all patent attorneys; it is known well by all those who engage in or are dealing with patents-that in the case of an article such as an electric light bulb, or in fact any other article of that type, there are constant new parts or patents or inventions being made.
I hold under my hand a statement giving a list of these numbered patents to which I formerly referred. I shall read only a few so as to indicate their variety. Hon. members will recall that the notice given to the dealer who imported was given under a certain list of 62 patents which were therein named. These 62 patents covered articles along these lines-and I shall not read all of them, because they are contained on two full sheets of foolscap; I shall read only a few so as to give the committee an idea of their complicated nature. They are sealing-in wires, methods of making tungsten wires, metal filaments, incandescent lamps, tungsten alloys, electrical lamps, base for incandescent lamps, filament supports, process of manufacturing non-sagging helical bodies of highly refractory metals-that's a mouthful. Then the list goes on: Multiple of incandescent lamps, tipless incandescent lamps, process for sealing

in wires, appliance for forming filaments, stem making machine, tipless incandescent electric lamp, and so on.
I shall not read them all. The point is that if during the period of three years or about the expiration of that time another patent is added to those entering into the manufacture of the lamp, then the individual cannot apply for another three years. And if during that three years another patent is secured and applied to the manufacture of this lamp he is put off for another three years.
I am told by competent authorities that that three year clause in the bill virtually make impossible the steps indicated in subsection (I) of section 65.
If the committee were interested I could outline others of these patents. They run from 1916 down to the present date. Almost every intervening year between 1916 and 1933 showed patents invoked in the courts by this company to stop the firm in question from selling the lamps. I am not dealing with theory; I am dealing with cases. Mr. Chairman, is it not recognized by the committee that when you say the attorney general of Canada or any other person may at any time after the expiration of three years make application that the likelihood or possibility of doing that is practically nil?
Now we shall proceed with the section, from that point. Subsection (2) reads:
The exclusive rights under a patent shall be deemed to have been abused in any of the following circumstances.
I shall not read them all, because most, of them are designed very definitely to protect the rights of patentees and do not constitute a protection of the public. I am not complaining about that but I merely dismiss the subject with that statement. One paragraph to which the minister referred a while ago I shall read, however, namely paragraph (c) of subsection 2.
(2) The exclusive rights under a patent shall be deemed to have been abused in any of the following circumstances:-
(c) if the demand for the patented' article in Canada is not being met to an adequate extent and on reasonable terms.
I direct the attention of the committee to the expressions " adequate extent " and "reasonable terms." What chance has any person to demonstrate those conditions when he is opposed by four great corporations, two of which are very large and two somewhat smaller. I submit that the possibility of proving that the public are not being adequately supplied would be impossible, because the chances are they would be. Then,

"reasonable terms"-what	are reasonable
terms? I submit that this abuse has been going on, and that a price of sixty cents is not a reasonable term. However it is allowed to go on, and nothing is done. Under the old act there was power to deal with the matter, but nothing was done. Attention was called to it, and still nothing was done. Therefore I say I am justified in stating to-day that the difference between thirty cents for the imported article, after paying the duty, and sixty cents for the domestic article is considered in Canada reasonable terms. I submit those are not reasonable terms, and that any company in Canada which receives a protection of 40 per cent should be able to operate on that basis. In the present instance I believe the protection is 40 per cent; the Minister of National Revenue has the tariff at his fingertips, and he will correct me if I am wrong. Surely that is sufficient protection for any concern in Canada manufacturing incandescent lamps. I do not object to protecting Canadian industry, having in mind the extent of the American market as compared with the Canadian market, and the cost of mass production as compared with more limited production. I have no objection to that at all, but I do submit that 40 per cent is sufficient. I go further, however; if it is not sufficient, then let us put the protection in the customs tariff, where it ought to be. Let us come before parliament, raise the tariff and give our reasons for it. But do not give permission to a great corporation or group of corporations to secure a protection amounting to 150 per cent or 200 per cent, in the guise of a patent right.
One point further: It will be noted that so far as I can find this is the only protection taking the place of the old act. I confess that I am a layman and am not supposed to understand the law, but so far as I can understand it I can find no obligation resting upon the commissioner to whom this application is to be made to give any decision in the matter at all. It may be there, but so far as I have been able to read it, I cannot find where the commissioner is called upon to .make any finding in the matter. It must be remembered that the appeal is by the attorney general of Canada or by any interested person to the commissioner of patents. That is the form of the appeal, and it must be proved that the products are not sold on reasonable terms. But there is no obligation on the commissioner to do anything in the mattar at all. What I submit is that so outstanding and so glaring is this abuse of the patent law that there ought to be in this new act a very definite section,
something that will be beyond all cavil and beyond all possibility of evasion that will deal with this situation. This is not the first time that I have had this matter up, and I do urge now as a member of this house, as I have done before, that this committee should before this bill passes take the necessary steps to have this abuse of privilege removed and reasonable protection given to the consumer in regard to this matter and, of course, in regard to other matters to which for the moment I do not choose to refer.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman,
that we all appreciate heartily what the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) has just said because it means so much to the Canadian people. Patents are a great handicap on our industries in this country. They are similar in their effects to an excessive tariff from which we receive no revenue. There are in this country subsidiaries of large American firms. Go to some of the smaller shoe factories in Toronto, for instance, and inquire what machines on the floor of their factory they own. You will find that in many of our Canadian cities our factories are using American machines and on that machine they pay royalties. The royalty is of two kinds: one is a time royalty and the other is a utility royalty, and in case the firm sells shoes below a certain price the American firm has the power so to adjust the time royalty or the utility royalty as to fix the price at which those shoes shall be sold. We are at the mercy of these large American concerns with subsidiaries in this country, just as the hon. member has said. They have their hand on the levers of our factories, and they dictate the price at which we shall sell our products by adjusting the royalties on their patents. What is more, while it brings in no revenue to this country, it results in centralizing our manufactures. There was a time when mowers and binders and other agricultural implements were made in our rural towns and villages, but patents have gradually destroyed these industries in our rural towns, and the manufacturing of these implements has become centralized in such large firms as the Massey-Harris Company. There we have a large dinosaur, one of those animals that have grown so large that they have ceased to be useful. It is almost impossible for the Massey-Harris Company to manufacture a few implements only. They have to manufacture them by the thousand because their plant has been built up for the purpose of doing an export trade, and at the present time our export trade is largely destroyed. I am sure that
Patents of Invention

any official of the Massey-Harris Company would tell you that the big plant of the Massey-Harris Company in Toronto cannot manufacture a binder as cheaply as it could be manufactured in the rural towns, and they will tell you that the reason is because of their large power requirements and the large labour force that is necessary to keep such a big plant going. In consequence they have to charge a higher price than we used to charge in our towns and villages when we were manufacturing these implements. I feel that patents and tariffs are great handicaps.

On section 1-Surrender of policy.

Inasmuch as I come from an industrial constituency, where a large number of people are out of work and are affected by the bill, I wish to say a word on their behalf. We hear a good deal about what the insurance companies have done for the people of this country, but we hear very little, if anything, of what the people have done for these companies. Ten years ago I contended that there should be a board of some sort over all such companies. I had on the order paper at that time a resolution to prevent them from taking trust funds and premiums and investing them in common stocks all over the world some of which stocks have proved since the depression nothing but South Sea bubbles. The government at that time did not see fit to adopt that proposed regulation, with the result that millions of dollars in premiums and trust funds invested the world over were lost in whole or in part not only investments by them on this continent but in all countries bordering on the seven seas. I have a bill also with reference to lapsed policies and the rates of interest thereon.
I submit that the house should adopt this bill because loan companies, mortgage companies, insurance companies and banks can no longer expect to receive the higher rates of interest which they have been charging in pre-depression days. This particular bill, by lowering interest rates and similar bills with reference to mortgages, loan companies and banks, would do more to get the people out of the mire than any other agency. It far transcends any other agency I can think of. Many skilled workmen, bricklayers, carpenters, plasterers and others have been out of work now for four or five years. When you talk about commercial rates, on insurance there is no commercial rate so far as these insurance companies are concerned. They are a law unto themselves. It was said on

Foreign Insurance Companies
April 12 that it would be interfering with the credit of the banks and with their business if we passed this bill. Now when a person is in financial difficulties the first agency he gets in touch with is a chartered bank, and the banks are a very important institution in the riding I represent. The policyholder gets a loan from a bank first and so cannot borrow from an insurance company after on a policy. Even bank managers cannot lend a hundred dollars to a retail merchant without authority from head office. If they do no one knows what they charge; they do not charge seven per cent because there is no adequate check or regulation governing them. These insurance companies are largely a law unto themselves. I have before me the annual report of the superintendent of insurance, which contains many quite interesting pages, giving the investments of every company in the country and throughout the world. It seems to me that the time is coming in Canada when the two old parties cannot fail to see the handwriting on the wall, because the working classes will not stand more of these high rates, whether they are charged by banks, mortgage companies, loan companies or by shark loan companies incorporated by this parliament in the last six or seven years and which cannot, by the widest stretch of the imagination be regarded as works for the general advantage of Canada. They get their charters from parliament and then go back and charge enormous rates of interest.
Again, I urge that there should be a federal regulation board over these insurance companies. In 1924 I proposed a trade commission which would take cognizance of such companies and have power to regulate them and their investments. Would it not have been a blessing if we had had a board before the depression of that sort which could have regulated investments in common stocks of insurance companies throughout the world? It would have saved the policyholders in losses by the companies hundreds of thousands and even millions of dollars.
I would point out that during the last few years rapid strides have been made in preventive medicine, science and surgery, as well as in many other departments of public health. Years ago there was no inspection of either milk or food or restaurants or abattoirs, but health departments everywhere have discovered the value of preventive medicine, with the result that the death rate has declined very appreciably indeed. I have returns from the federal United States health department disclosing some interesting figures, 92582-198
but I will not take that up to-night; instead I want to refer to the University of Toronto monthly, May issue. Referring to this particular problem, it says:
It is interesting to compare the expectation of life at the end of 1933 with that at the end of 1929 and earlier periods. The expectation of life at birth in 1911 and 1912 was 46.63 years; in 1919 and 1920, 51.14 years; in 1929, 55.78 years; and in 1933 it had reached the level of 59.19 years. It is evident that the upward trend of improvement has continued in spite of hard times.
The rates of insurance in this country are altogether too high and the dividends allowed in reduction of premium per annum are not as much as they should be. The inspection of these companies is also not what it should be. In the United States an investigation into Wall street and banks, insurance and brokers and stock companies, was conducted by the United States senate. We have in this country to-day a senate that is nothing but an anachronism. If the Canadian senate had done work similar to that which the United States senate did two years ago we would never have required a mass buying committee. The people of this country want relief from the high rates charged by mortgage companies, loan companies, banks, and insurance companies; such institutions cannot expect in the future to get the high returns or high money which they have always collected in the past. The day of "high" money has gone, in view of the borrowing by the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities and in view of the action taken by the banks in reducing the rate of interest on their depositors' moneys. All the money which the banks have to lend is their depositors' money and all the moneys which the insurance companies have to lend is the premiums paid by the policyholders or trust funds.
This bill is a step in the right direction and I am hoping in the future something further may be done along the lines of benefit to the working people in the matter also. Some people are always talking about what these foreign and domestic insurance companies have done for this country. What have they done to pull this country out of the mire? Have they done anything about housing or construction? No. Have they done anything in the way of lending money for reconstruction? No. T^iey are making it all the harder for small business men to borrow money on real estate investments and other forms of securities. At Gravesend Beach, Brooklyn, New York, the New York Life has lent $25,000,000 for the building of small homes and flats for the benefit of the working

31 IS

Foreign Insurance Companies
classes who live on that particular island. It has lent that money without any federal, state or municipal assistance. In view of all the policyholders have done for that company, it is trying to do something to pull the United States out of the mire by lending this money in the hope that it will create work for some of the policyholders who cannot pay their annual premiums and for skilled workmen, to take them off the dole. In that way the New York Life is trying to do something for its policyholder's; it is trying to create work on that island, to relieve the housing and reconstruction situation and to come to the help of the government. Did anyone ever hear of an insurance company, foreign or domestic, in this country coming to the help of the federal government or the provinces or the municipalities? No; they are hoarding up all this wealth to spend it without the proper regulation which there should be over these companies as they like. In the session of 1927, when the late Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance, I proposed that there should be some regulation over these companies. He was a very good minister for the people, and at that time when I sat on the other side of the house, I asked him why there should not be a revision of the insurance law every ten years just as there was of the Bank Act. I asked him: Did he propose to wait until there was an episode similar to that of the Home bank among the insurance companies before any adequate modern insurance legislation would be passed to control these companies with proper inspection and regulation.
As regards these mortgage companies, loan companies, some of these shark loan companies that are operating in the city from which I come and that have been chartered by this parliament, and some of whom, as the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) says, are charging as high as 42 per cent-I can tell them that the day of "high" money is gone by. In view of the depression, the insurance companies instead of issuing pamphlets to influence members of parliament would be doing something in the right direction if they lent money for housing and reconstruction, and reduced rates all along the line. As a policyholder in these companies I have received a document which I think is an intimidation of a member of parliament. It is published by the president of the Canadian Life Insurance Officers' Association under date of April 26 last and is addressed to me as a policyholder and as a member of the house. It reads:
An important measure is before the house m which you are directly interested as a

member of the house and doubtless as the holder of a life insurance policy as well. We refer to the proposal to reduce the rate of interest charged on policy loans.
Most of the members have no doubt received a copy of this printed document which is headed:
Memorandum with respect to the rate of interest charged on loans on . life insurance policies.
The headings of the different paragraphs are:
1.	Policy loans not ordinary loans; life insurance companies not bankers.
2.	Interest rate in policy contract applicable long distance into future.
3.	Lowering interest rate injurious to policyholders.
4.	Danger of "run" on insurance companies.
There could be a much greater danger or
a " run " on some of them the way they invested in common stock the world over.
5.	Companies would be forced to change investment policies.
6.	Low interest rate wouid encourage borrowing for speculative purposes.
7.	Policy loans work to disadvantage of companies.
8.	Heavy expense involved in handling policy loans, individual policy loans small.
9.	Policy values required to be reduced.
I look on this as nothing but an effort to intimidate a member of parliament by urging him by these reasons addressed to him as a policyholder. These particular gentlemen who are the officers of these companies are simply trustees for these funds. They have invested in common stocks the world over without any adequate regulation and with an utter contempt for the policyholders whose funds they administer with great loss to the company. Not only should this bill pass, but we should have similar ones in regard to the banks, loan companies and mortgage companies. If we did something like that, we would be encouraging the building of houses and reconstruction in a way that would make a good effort toward bringing the people of this country out of the mire.

May I say just a few words in suppprt of this bill which I introduced some time ago? It was changed in the banking committee and was reprinted. I am given to understand that the reprinted bill has not been generally distributed among the members, and if there is a supply of copies on the table, I would suggest that the reprinted bill should be made available to the members of the committee. It is not on my file and some of the members have told me it is not on theirs, and so that the members may not be under any misapprehension, I hope the reprinted bill will be distributed.

Foreign Insurance Companies
This matter of the rate of interest which should be charged on policy loans was very carefully considered in the banking and commerce committee. We had several sessions of the committee; the life insurance companies were .well represented by a delegation of insurance men, with very eminent counsel to speak for them. I regret that the insurance companies when they circularized1 the members of the house did not include me in the list; I did not get one of the circulars to which the last speaker referred. May I put the matter briefly to the committee in this way; first I would stress the importance of this matter to the people of Canada who are forced to borrow on their life insurance policies-

Before my hon. friend proceeds, he says, and it is true as far as I am concerned, that this amended bill is not on, our files. It seems to me that we should adjourn the consideration of this important matter until we have the bill before us. I do not know whether I am in order in moving that the committee rise, but I think it is only right that we should have the bill before us. If I am in order I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Before you put that
motion, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the reprinted bills have been distributed to the desks but not put on the files. I found mine beside my file.

These bills are not reprinted when amended. I have read the section. It is an amendment to the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, and provides that interest shall be at the rate of five per cent. The original draft said1 four per cent.

It is most unusual that these
amendments are not before us. I do not think it ever happened before that the chairman merely read the amended clause and the committee dealt with it.
Could we have a statement of the exact position? I confess that I am at a loss.

The
bill is No. 14. I shall read the original clauses which went to the banking and commerce committee:
1. The Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932, as amended by chapter thirty-six of the statutes of 1934, is further amended by inserting the following section therein immediately after section thirty-nine thereof:-
39a. (1) In the case of life companies, whenever any holder of a policy other than a term or natural premium policy has paid three or 92582-1981
more annual premiums thereon or their equivalent half-yearly or quarterly premiums and fails to pay any further premium or desires to surrender the policy, the premiums paid shall not be forfeited, but he shall be entitled to receive a paid-up and commuted policy for such sum as the directors ascertain and determine, or to be paid in cash such sum as the directors fix as the surrender value of the policy; such sum in either case to be ascertained upon principles to be adopted by by-law applicable generally to all such cases as occur, or extended insurance under the policy for a period proportionate to such cash surrended value.
That clause was deleted in its entirety by the banking and commerce committee. Then clause 2 of the original bill read:
(2)	The sums so ascertained and the duration for which insurance may be extended, based upon the assumption that the policy is not subject to any lien by way of loan or otherwise, shall be inserted in the policy and form a p_art of the contract between the company and the insured.
That was also deleted.
(3)	In the event of the policy being subject to any such lien when default is made in payment of a premium as aforesaid, such lien shall be taken into account in fixing the cash surrender value and the paid-up and commuted policy herein referred to.
That was also deleted.
(4)	Until the policyholder elects to accept such cash surrender value or such paid-up and commuted policy, such cash surrender value shall be applied by the company to maintain the policy in force at its full face value until the whole of the surrender value under the policy is exhausted.
That was also deleted.
Is it not a fact that the original bill was all deleted except one clause?
Yes.
Many hon. members have objected to clauses which they read from their files, which clauses have already been deleted.

Well, if I may just finish: Under clause 5 as originally drafted interest was to be payable at the rate of four per cent per annum on loans on insurance policies. That was changed and the present bill substituted. The bill was reprinted as reported from the committee. The reprint places the rate of interest at five per cent, defines interest, and also fixes a period of time, saying that the section shall not apply to any loan or unpaid balance thereof made under an agreement executed or advanced automatically under any policy issued before January 1, 1936.

In view of the explanation made and1 the very great
Foreign Insurance Companies

change that is (proposed, I think this bill ought to 'be distributed to the members before it is further considered, and that it should stand over for that purpose.
I move that the committee rise.
I understood-
This motion is not debatable.

But there is a point of order involved. I understood the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) to rise to a point of order, but after he raised the point, of order he made a motion. I suggest that that procedure is not available to any hon. member of this committee. I relinquished the floor to the hon. member only because he said he was raising a point of order. If there is a point of order involved I should like to know what it is. This bill was amended in. the committee and was ordered to be reprinted. I simply suggested that apparently the reprint was not available to all the members, but the bill has been reprinted; the reprints must be in existence somewhere. It was for the information of hon. members that I suggested that the copies might now be distributed to hon. members who have not got them. The bill was passed by the banking and commerce committee long ago; surely we might now consider it.
I have to call the hon. member to order; the motion is not debatable.

Well, I raise the point of order that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough raised a point of order and after he had thus succeeded in getting the floor he made a motion, which procedure was not in order.
The motion has been renewed since, and it is now before the committee.

But surely I should have the right to the floor when it was taken from me in that way. I suggest that I have the floor until some hon. member can prove a point of order. I am in your hands, Mr. Chairman.
