I should like first to ask the officers of the house if there are not plenty of copies of this bill available. It is difficult

enough for any private member to get a public bill through this house; we have only two hours a week, and then private bills take precedence. The motion has been made and is before the chair.

How can it be before the
chair if the rules are properly enforced? How did I lose the floor except that the hon. member raised a point of order which I suggest was absolutely wrong? I suggest that I have the floor now and that no motion can properly have been made, when the debate was interrupted simply on a point of order. No disposition was ever made of the point of order.

On the point of order, I am
quite willing for my hon. friend to continue his speech, but he put the words in my mouth and I thought I was helping him out. He said there was no bill before the house. I thought that by raising the point of order and moving that the committee rise I wTas helping the hon. member out in his argument. I was simply trying to suggest to the committee the importance of this bill to a certain class of people in Canada, those policyholders who are finding it difficult to keep their premiums paid, some of whom have had to borrow money to keep their policies in good standing. In the banking committee the superintendent of insurance told us that before this act was introduced rates running all the way from six per cent to ten per cent were being charged by insurance companies in Canada on policy loans.

Foreign Insurance Companies
I certainly think this is a matter on which this house should come to a decision and in connection with which we should lay down a maximum rate of interest which the insurance companies may charge.
These companies were very well represented before the banking committee by very able counsel, and this section of the bill was passed by a good majority, setting the minimum rate at five per cent. If the reduction meant only one per cent-and it means more than that -it would mean a saving of $2,500,000 to certain policyholders who are borrowers. The companies cannot earn a rate of six per cent on any other investment they can make today. Certainly they cannot net six per cent on their mortgage investments; I doubt if they can net five per cent. Why they should want to charge their own policyholders on guaranteed loans like this-as a matter of fact the policyholders are only borrowing their own money-a higher rate of interest than they can earn on any other class of investment is quite beyond my understanding. Last year one of the biggest companies in Canada averaged 4-08 per cent on all their investments. If they have any money coming in to-day to invest in dominion government bonds they cannot earn much more than three per cent. Why charge the poor policyholder who wants to borrow at a rate of six per cent? Some companies charge seven per cent and others charge even more.

I should
like to ask the hon. member a question. What will be the effect on the profits of the policyholders who do not borrow if the rate of interest on loans to policyholders is reduced?

I think the net result would
be to reduce their earnings by a very small fraction indeed. Let me suggest this to the hon. member: Why should any policyholders who do not need to borrow want to make this inordinate profit out of the poor policyholders who do need to borrow, and who are really only borrowing their own money? I know it has been suggested, and it has been stated in newspaper articles, that we are in danger of ruining the insurance companies by setting the rate so low that all the policyholders will want to borrow money. That is rank nonsense. Why, the insurance companies were pretending to lend money at one per cent less than the banks, years ago, and there was no run on the insurance companies for money. Who is going to borrow from the insurance companies rather than the banks simply because he can get the money at one-half per cent or one per cent less? I am told that to-day a good deal of money is being lent
by the chartered banks at five per cent, and the chartered banks of Canada cannot have loans as safe as the loans that are made by insurance companies to their own policyholders. The companies cannot possibly lose. Why should we allow them to charge a higher rate of interest than anyone else in Canada is able to earn, and higher than they can get anywhere else in Canada? For the life of me I cannot understand that. I do not believe any class of people in this country want to borrow on their insurance policies unless it is necessary. Most of the people who borrow, so the superintendent of insurance told us, are small policyholders who borrow to keep their policies intact, or to keetp their houses from being sold over their heads, or to keep themselves off relief. As a matter of fact today the insurance companies 'are handling approximately as much of the savings of the Canadian people as the chartered banks are handling. We have compelled the chartered banks to reduce their interest, through the legislation passed last year. They have reduced the interest to their savings depositors, and I think we must secure a general lowering of interest rates all along the line wherever it is possible. Here is one place where it is possible.
One of the companies making a strong fight against this bill has used the money of the policyholders in a way that I do not think would be approved by any of us. They have put $21,000,000 into a head office building, yet some of the men connected with that company would say, "You will ruin us if you put us in a position where we have to lend the policyholders all the money they want to borrow at a rate as low as five per cent." They have millions of dollars invested in bonds that do not yield more than three and a half per cent; they have millions of dollars invested in the bonds of countries other than Canada that are not worth fifty cents on the dollar; t'hey have millions of dollars invested in industrial stocks and bonds that are not worth fifty cents on the dollar. The other day one man said to me that perhaps one reason they are fighting this measure is that they need this rate of interest to make up their losses through bad investments. So far as I am concerned I do not propose that they should be allowed to charge more than five per cent to mlake up their losses in other ways. I do not know why they want a higher rate. We have life insurance in Canada for the benefit of the people, not for the benefit of these great companies, and by this bill we are not endangering any company. We know this government would not allow any insurance company to fail; we have had proof of that.
Foreign Insurance Companies

These companies have so much money coming in that they do not know what to do with it, but if anyone wants to borrow on his insurance in order to keep his premiums paid he must pay six per cent and in some cases eight per cent. The largest company in Canada charges eight per cent on automatic loans to-day, and only three months ago, up to the time this bill was introduced, one company was charging ten per cent. They stopped charging ten per cent simply because this bill was brought in.
I appeal to the members of this committee to quit fooling in connection with this bill and to vote on. it. If they do not want it they can vote it down; if they want it they can put it through, but the committee should not rise now when the bill can come up only twice a week. There are quite a number of public bills on the order paper; any time any members choose to put up a fight in connection with a divorce bill here it can go on for two or three weeks, and during that time we have no chance to consider any public bills introduced by private members. I appeal to the committee either to pass this bill or to turn it down. I do not want to indulge in any more argument; I rose to-night only because I thought perhaps there was some misunderstanding in connection with the bill. I know some of the members were looking at the old bill. I would not object to letting the bill stand if it was for the purpose of getting further information, but I think the main purpose in putting the bill over would be, "Well, if it is put .over to-night that is one less opportunity to discuss it." I do appeal to the members of the committee to pass the bill.

In this free parliament we are allowed to express our opinions freely, and there should not be any insinuations made with regard to what any member of this house thinks in regard to any measure coming before it. Of course I am not surprised that my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) should wind up his argument by practically trying to leave with the public the idea that certain members of this committee and this house do not want to have this matter properly discussed. The trouble with my hon. friend is that he seems to be going around in a circle. When he first rose to his feet fifteen or twenty minutes ago he told the committee that this .bill had not been reprinted. Until he made that statement I did not know whether or not it had been reprinted. I looked up my file immediately and found I did not have it. Some other hon. members sitting around me made the same statement, and consequently I felt- that before the matter

was further considered it was my duty, out of respect to hon. members who did not sit on the banking and commerce committee, to see that they had an opportunity to be seized of the facts, particularly when one bill went to the banking and commerce committee and a much different bill is now being discussed. I do not know why the hon. member should complain. It is true that the bill is important, and in view of its importance I move that the committee rise.

Before the bill passes to
a further stage I should like to say a few words. As it was first introduced and brought before the banking and commerce committee I found myself opposed to certain clauses. Now however I am just as much in favour of the clauses in the present bill. It seems to me ridiculous that including costs any man should be charged rates of 10 per cent or 12 per cent upon money which is rightly his. These loans are made only upon the surrender value of an insurance policy. If he chose, a man could surrender the policy and accept the money. On the other hand he may choose to borrow a few dollars for the purpose of keeping his policy in force or for other reasons, and in the past he has been charged seven per cent and in many cases much more. I say there is no security so ample as that given by the borrower; it is surer than Dominion of Canada bonds because, as I previously stated, the policyholder is borrowing his own money. The insurance companies are most anxious to keep it that way; they do not wish to have policies surrendered, and at the same time they are attempting to secure much greater interest than they could possibly secure from the best securities they hold. I am in favour of the reduction in the rate of interest, and would1 be content to vote for even a larger reduction.

Question.

Foreign Insurance Companies
Mr. Chairman, this matter has been discussed at least by some hon. members of the committee as if it were a case between insurance companies and borrowers.
That is what it is.

I submit that is not the
position at all. As I understand the situation, insurance companies receive ten per cent of the profits which are made, the balance of the profits going to the policyholders. It seems to me now, as it seemed to me before the banking and commerce committee, that the bill might more properly be opposed by policyholders than by the companies. The companies which were there at that time, I take it, were representing the great mass of policyholders who were not borrowers, rather than the companies themselves, because as I say they are very little interested in the rate of interest received.
Are not these borrowers who continue to be policyholders as much interested as anybody else?

Yes; I shall deal with
that in a moment. Speaking for myself, I am representing a policyholder and I believe representing quite a mass of policyholders who are not in favour of trust funds which have been created for the protection of their wives and children being exposed to compulsory borrowing by people who may wish to use it for other than emergency purposes.
In the first place my point is that the insurance companies are not vitally interested in this bill, but that those who are interested are the mass of policyholders who have placed their fund's in insurance companies in order that their wives and children might be protected. It seems to me we are getting off on the wrong foot when we speak of it as if it were a battle between insurance companies and borrowers. It seems to me, in the second place, that we are regarding this bill as having something to do with the general movement afoot in Canada to reduce interest rates. I am in favour of the reduction of interest rates both on commercial and on mortgage loans, but I would hasten to point out, if I may, that this is not in the same class. These loans are compulsory loans which must toe made and which cannot be refused by the companies and they are made out of trust funds accumulated for the benefit of dependents of the policyholders. It seems to me they are in an entirely different category from loans made by commercial banks, or mortgage companies from which' we expect1 and want to get the lowest possible rates.
The fund which has been created is one which has been paid in by policyholders throughout the dominion. I learned from figures given a few days ago in an address delivered by the Secretary of State that policies aggregating about six billions of dollars are outstanding in Canada. This fund has been created by the great mass of policyholders in order that their wives and children may be protected. The proposal now is to make it as easy as possible for any policyholder to come in and say to a company, "I want you to lend me money at four per cent," or five per cent, as the case may be, notwithstanding the fact that he may have to pay six per cent to a bank.
Is it not the business of insurance companies to invest their funds to the best possible advantage?
It is.
Is there any safer loan at a greater remuneration than five per cent?

They have a perfect right to invest their funds in any security which they think fit and which falls within the terms of the act. But the first duty of an insurance company is not to make money on its loans but to see to it that funds are liquid and available for payment to beneficiaries under policies. That is the principle which I submit may not be observed if it is made easy for policyholders to compel insurance companies to give loans on policies at low rates.
I gave an example in the banking and commerce committee. It seems to me that if Mr. A has paid in money on his policy and expects his wife and children to benefit from those payments, in the event of anything happening to him, he has some interest in seeing that Mr. B is not encouraged to draw out money from the company and thus to deplete the fund. He is interested in seeing that Mr. B is not encouraged by being able to go to the company and obtain a loan at a rate lower than that at which he could obtain a loan from a bank.

In the alternative the policyholder who is desirous of borrowing could withdraw all his interest in the policy. The policyholder who desired to borrow a small sum could, if he chose, take the cash surrender value of the policy.

I do not wish to make it any easier for me or anyone else who is a policyholder to get the money out. I submit what we should do is not to encourage but to discourage borrowing on policies. While it

Foreign Insurance Companies
is true that from time to time in selling policies companies stress the point that the policyholder will be able to borrow money on his policy, it seems to me that that is not the primary purpose for which a policy is written; it is not the primary purpose for which a policy is sought. The principle of protection, is the one which should govern, rather than the principle of being able to get ready money through a loan on the policy.
I suggest we should be careful to see to it that any person who borrows on a policy is not encouraged to do so by reason of the fact .that he can get the money at a cheaper interest rate than could be obtained at a bank. Mr. B should not be encouraged to borrow. The general principle should be kept in mind that borrowing on insurance policies should be for emergency and not for commercial purposes. I believe hon. members of this committee know that during the boom time of 1929 and early 1930, a good deal of borrowing on policies was done which should not have been done. That borrowing was carried on, however, because it was easy to get money on account of an insurance policy. If the rate of interest is such that it makes it expensive to borrow there is at least a deterrent, a brake, if not a complete bar to the borrowing on these .policies. I submit that if we make it easy to borrow on insurance policies it means in some cases that in times of stress and strain we may have a situation such as arose in the United States not very long ago, when the government itself had to step in and prevent borrowing on insurance policies in order to save the companies from liquidation. What does this mean? It means that if a company gets a run on its policies by reason of the fact of a loan being obtainable at a low rate of interest, it will have to dump its securities to meet these loans, and this endangers the very trust fund of which that company is trustee for the benefit of the policyholders and beneficiaries. It is not a quetsion of the interest of the .companies. It is a question of the interest of the mass of policyholders. It is not a question of a general reduction in interest rates. It is a question whether or not we shall, as far as we can, preserve intact a fund that has been created primarily, not for the purpose of being drawn on from time to time for ordinary commercial purposes, but for the protection of the wives and children of policyholders.

May I ask the hon. member
who has just taken his seat (Mr. Ralston), who seems to be well up in this subject,

which I am not, what .would be the effect upon the companies who have group insurance if members of such groups of industrial workers were allowed to borrow on such policies? Would not the withdrawal of one seriously affect the position of the whole group?

I am not in a position
to answer that question. I do not know whether under group insurance policies contain the privilege of borrowing or not. I rather imagine they do.
Not for individuals.
Not for individuals, I should think.

I was much impressed with the arguments of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) in support .of this bill, but there was one point on which I would have to disagree with him. He said that insurance should be for the benefit of the insured, if I heard him aright. I do not think so. I think it is for the benefit of the beneficiaries. I understand that a man's life insurace is almost the only asset he can leave to his wife and family of which his creditors cannot deprive him, and if you make it easier for the creditors to get hold of that insurance policy I do not think you are going to benefit the beneficiaries in any way. The creditors cannot take the insurance away from the wife and family, but they can go to the man himself and say, "Why are you paying us seven per cent interest when you can borrow from the insurance company at five per cent? Why not borrow on your policy and pay us off?" They might induce him to borrow from the insurance company and thus take away from his wife and family an asset that the creditors could not touch in any other way. For that reason I think this bill should be opposed.

It seems to me that the crux of this bill lies in the question of fixing interest rates. I think it would be very unwise to fix interest rates at the present time. At no other time in the history of economics have interest rates been so uncertain as they are at present, and no one can. tell what interest rates will be six months or a year from now. Most life insurance policies are issued for long terms, twenty or thirty or forty years, and to pass a bill fixing interest rates at any given figure I think would be unwise. The insurance companies are bound by their policies to make these loans when they are requested; they cannot refuse them; they have to make them, and if they have to make

them at the rate of five per cent when money might be at six or seven per -cent it is not very hard to understand how the insurance companies would soon be called upon- to act the part of bankers. The insurance companies would then have to keep liquid reserves to a far greater extent than they do at the present time. They would have to invest their money in such a way that it could be -called on if necessary. I am told that in the United States there was an insurance company, perhaps more than one,, that wias in a very serious position during this last depression because of a run on the company for loans on its policies. If t-his bill were to pass, the insurance companies would then be competing with banks an-d loan companies in making small loans.
Something has been -said about the insurance companies -charging eight per cent. I understand that it is a six per cent interest rate an-d a charge of two per cent for service. It seems to me that a more equitable charge for service would have been a -certain fixed charge per month levied by the insurance company, instead of a .percentage rate, and had that been the -case I think we would never have heard of an eight per -cent interest rate being charged. The companies do not want this business. I would be in favour of -denying the right to the policyholder to borrow on his policy, rather than put this bill through and fix the interest rate. If this bill passed, the effect undoubtedly w-ould be to increase the number of -loans and -possibly the amounts of the loans, particularly if the ordinary interest rate rose. The borrowings would then be so large, as has been sta-t-ed, that instead of being an insurance company it would foe merely a ba-nker in charge of bank accounts which might be drawn upon- to the full extent at any moment.
The insurance companies are charged with levying high interest rates. I am told that six per cent is now the ruling rate, and that rate was fixed by the insurance companies in agreement among themselves before this bill was presented to the house. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the more w-e interfere in matters of this kind the harder we shall make it for insurance companies to carry on their work.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was about to rise to reply to certain remarks of the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens). I wish to emphasize again that this bill as it is now before the house, with the exception of two or three verbal amendments, which are due perhaps to the negligence of the printer or draftsman, was approved after nineteen sittings of the banking and commerce committee of the senate and after an investigation of the facts unprecedented in my experience in respect of any public bill of this nature. I appreciate the fact that the hon. gentleman received from someone information with regard to an alleged grievance in respect of patent rights on electric bulbs. If the party who suffered from an abuse or alleged grievance had addressed himself to the Secretary of State, even under the existing act, I am sure I could have suggested administrative measures which would have served to overcome the abuse specified; or if the person suffering from the abuse had applied to the commissioner for an investigation under the existing act, I am satisfied that remedial measures could have been obtained which would have afforded very considerable redress at least.
The number of elements in an electric light bulb is seven: (1) a base; (2) the globe; (3) a filament support; (4) lead-in wires; (5) an alloy for a filament; (6) a getter for the removal of gases during the baking of the filament within the lamp; (7) the sealing of the lamp. How there could be with respect to one type of bulb some sixty odd patents outstanding surpasses my comprehension. The hon. gentleman suggested that under the bill before the house the term of three years is given during which the patentee may erect his factory, equip it with machinery and proceed with the manufacture of the article in respect of which the patent subsists, and he said that with regard to any patented article the fact that improvements may be patented from time to time renders it impossible to revoke the patent or to give compulsory licences to third parties to manufacture under any patent because of the oontinued improvements made from year to year. This argument is fallacious at least in this respect, that a commissioner or the exchequer court under the old act or under the present proposed consolidated act could in case of abuse license the manufacture of any type of bulb up to the last improvement-and improvements are not so rapid in the manufacture of electric bulbs that the manufacturer, under all the patents existing for three years before the application, might not manufacture a very
Patents of Invention

excellent bulb which would prove satisfactory under most conditions and circumstances. But my hon. friend, if I understood him aright, referred to the three year clause as an evil which should be remedied by the measure now before the house. Let me say first that the three years is given from the date of the granting of the patent within which the patentee may proceed with the proposed manufacture by erection of his factory and the equipment of it with machinery; and that three year provision exists in the Patent Act of every leading country in the world. It has been found by experience in all countries that, if an average term is to be fixed, three years is the most satisfactory, and in fact so satisfactory has that term been found that in the international convention for the protection of industrial property, which was signed at the Hague on November 6, 1925, and ratified by Canada on May 1, 1928, and which convention is adhered to by nearly every leading country in the world, it is provided in article 5 that there shall be at least a term of three years within which the patentee shall be allowed to proceed in his preliminary arrangements for the manufacture of the article patented. Article 5 provides:
The importation by the patentee into the country where the patent has been granted of articles manufactured in any of the countries of the union shall not entail revocation of the patent; nevertheless each of the contracting countries shall have the right to take the necessary legislative measures to prevent the abuses which might result from the exercise of the exclusive rights conferred by the patent, for example, failure to work.
These measures shall not provide for the revocation of the patent unless the grant of compulsory licences is insufficient to prevent such abuses. In no case can the patent be made liable to such measures before the expiration of at least three years from the date of the grant of the patent.
That three year period, which is accepted by all leading countries in the world, is the period we are bound to grant under the international convention to which we are now parties. But when we sought to find remedial measures against possible abuses which might arise, and remedial measures which are within the terms of the international convention to which we are parties, we turned to the latest revision of the Patent Act of the United Kingdom. We sought to take advantage of the vast store of experience which the patent office of the United Kingdom has acquired. Since this convention was framed and ratified by the United Kingdom as well as by Ganada there has been a revision of the Patent Act of the United Kingdom in which they have provided very satisfactory and, I think,

salutory and efficient measures to overcome the abuses which may develop from the patent monopoly. So that the senate has adopted verbatim, at the suggestion of the department of the Secretary of State and the patent office, the provisions which are now found in sections 65, 66, 67, 68 and 69 of this bill. In respect of these sections, though only two of them are now before the committee, I may say by way of explanation that the English provision is in one section, section 27, a very lengthy section; and in order to facilitate references to it we divided that section 27 into four parts. Therefore section 65 of this bill is identical with subsections 1 and 2 of section 27 of the English patent act, with one exception, Under the English act any person interested may apply to the commissioner in case of an abuse, but in Canada; so widespread in territory, we have introduced one slight change, namely, giving to the attorney general of the dominion the right to take proceedings ab initio. It is desirable, I think, to maintain responsible government in this country and to provide not only that the Secretary of State shall be responsible to the government of which he is a member and to parliament in respect of the administration of the act, but that the Attorney General of Canada shall be responsible in respect to the initiation of proceedings to abolish or to remedy abuses arising under the act.
I do not wish to state personal opinions in dealing with a government measure such as this, but my own view is that in framing general acts to deal with prevalent evils, a mistake would foe made if you should attempt by general acts to deal with specific instances which have arisen, and which can be remedied by an efficient administration of the general act by the person responsible to the government and to parliament of such administration. The enactment of general laws is necessary, but with regard to the administration of general acts, in my experience, the end may be accomplished by establishing that ministers of the crown in certain capacities shall be directly responsible to the crown and to parliament for the efficient administration of those acts. That principle or policy we have endeavoured to incorporate in the bill now before the committee.

I understand also that
alternatively any person interested still has, as well as the attorney general, a right to appeal.

3. It is declared with relation to every naragraph of the next foregoing subsection that, for the purpose of determining whether there has been any abuse of the exclusive rights under a patent, it shall be taken that patents, for new inventions are granted not only to encourage invention but to secure that new inventions shall so far as possible be worked on a commercial scale in Canada without undue delay.

If the commissioner is satisfied that the objects of this and the last foregoing sections cannot be attained by the exercise of any of the foregoing powers-
That is, powers which are given to them of granting involuntary licences to other competitors and the like.
-he may order the patent to be revoked, either forthwith or after such reasonable interval as may be specified in the order, unless in the meantime such conditions as may be prescribed in the order with a view to attaining the objects of this and the last foregoing sections are fulfilled.
That .is a very arbitrary power; it is nevertheless a power which may be exercised in case the patentee abuses the rights which are conferred upon him. I may not have the opportunity or privilege of enforcing this new measure, but I say with perfect confidence in view of my experience in connection with the patent office for the last four and a half or nearly five years, that in the terms of this proposal I can find remedies, adequate remedies, for every abuse which has been brought to my notice during that time. I am sure that if my successor will make himself thoroughly conversant with these terms, and if he is supported by the government of which he is a member, he can find adequate remedies for such abuses as those of which the hon. member for East Kootenay has complained. With that sincere conviction, and in view of the time that has been given to the framing of these provisions and to securing their consistent application to the objeots which we have in view, I trust that the House of Commons at this late date will not undertake any haphazard amendment of this bill.

July 30, 1934. About the first week in August I found on my desk a letter which is no doubt the letter to which the hon. gentleman refers. It was a matter with respect to which I thought there should be some consultation with him and with the law officers of the crown. I made inquiry and I found that my hon. friend had left Ottawa for the west and it was then useless for me to write and send after him letters addressed to a destination which I did not know, and I did not meet- the hon. gentleman again imtil late in the autumn; I think it was late in October.

Was that immediately
after the by-elections that he conducted in Ontario?

I did not meet him immediately after those by-elections. The next time we met was late in certainly the latter part of October. In the meantime this complaint received very careful consideration and I will say that the fact of the complaint being made

was one reason why we adopted the changes which I have indicated in this bill in connection with its administration. I have had some experience with blue sky laws in the central western states of the United States, and after that experience I still believe in responsible government; that is, in the administration of public acts by members of the government who are responsible to their colleagues in the government and to parliament, and it would take a very great deal of argument to change my opinion in this respect.
If it is deemed advisable to place the administration of this act under some such board as my hon. friend indicates, then the proper way to introduce such administrative action is to constitute such a board and to state in the terms of the act constituting it what its powers are, otherwise such act wiould have no special reference to the administration of this act, which is administered by a commissioner under the supervision of a minister of the crown. But section 40 of the Patent act, as it now exists and then existed, did not permit either the minister or the commissioner taking cognizance of such an alleged abuse as that stated in the letter to which my hon. friend refers, except upon the filing of a petition by a person interested, and that is why we place now the responsibility upon the attorney general of Canada with regard to the institution of such proceedings. Section 40 of the existing act proceeds under Ob) to say:
Any person interested may present a petition to the commissioner alleging that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to a patented' invention have not been satisfied,
or that the patentee has failed to manufacture adequately the patented invention in Canada, and so forth. Under the present act the basis of the commissioner's action is the presentation of a petition to the commisioner, and the parties to whom my hon. friend has referred never presented a petition, never instituted proceedings. If they were aggrieved all' they had to do was to write a petition to the commissioner, not in formal terms but in any terms that came within the provisions of the act, alleging that these abuses existed. But there was no petition presented, and no such initiative taken in the letters which the hon. gentleman sent to the department with his letter, which I understand from my hon. friend was dated July 30. It certainly was received at my department, but only after my hon. friend had left Ottawa for his expedition into the west, and when I had no opportunity of consulting with him.
But in order that the department might have jurisdiction to deal with such matters

we have in this bill enlarged that section, as I have stated, by expressing that the attorney general of Canada or any person interested in the patent may initiate these proceedings, and that change is made for the express purpose of allowing a minister of the crown to bring the matter before the attorney general of Canada, who at the public expense can take the proceedings which heretofore depended upon private initiative. In making that change I think that we have obviated certain difficulties which have confronted us under the existing act.
As to the customs duties imposed upon electrical machinery and instruments I cannot discuss those at the present time. If they were very onerous, if they led to abuses, who rather than the Minister of Trade and Commerce should bring such matters to the attention of the government of the day, and although I sat assiduously in council I do not think I am violating any oath of office by saying that I do not recall at least, either in council or out of council, that my hon. friend ever brought such matters to the consideration of his colleagues.
But if there is any amendment which is now suggested to these clauses, why not let us have the suggested amendment and let us consider it on its merits. I tell this house with all the sincerity and faithfulness of which I am capable that I believe in adopting here the terms of the Patent Act which the long experience of the officers of the United Kingdom has found adequate to remedy just such or abuses similar to those complained of, adopting that very language, and then, by adding to the English Act the provision with regard to the attorney general of Canada taking initiative on behalf of the body politic at the expense of the treasury, I am going just as far as I can see that it is possible for us to go in providing efficient remedies.
I simply say again that under our Patent act as it is now proposed to be amended, with the cooperation of the attorney general of Canada as a colleague, I certainly believe that that act can be efficiently administered not only on the technical side, but also to compass the whole matter of commercial advantage which my hon. friends have in view. I cannot say any more than that. I am simply expressing my sincere opinion after four or five years' experience.
May I ask if by the attorney general in this act is meant the Minister of Justice?

Yes. The difficulty I had was to find in the old act some authority: on the part of the attorney general to intervene, and we have provided in several sections of this act that he may now intervene and initiate proceedings on behalf of the general body politic.

I would like to ask the minister a question or two for information. The hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) this afternoon and this evening cited a case where an importer had imported electric bulbs into this country and had been communicated with by the solicitors of the Canadian General Electric, who pointed out to him that these bulbs imported into this country were an infringement of the patent rights of the General Electric. I do not know what has been the final result of that communication, but the question I want to put to the Secretary of State is this. Suppose the General Electric Company in the United States controls the larger volume or a very large volume of the patents in connection with electric bulbs; suppose it creates a company in Canada, the Canadian General Electric, to which it transfers the right to manufacture from patents owned by the parent company in the United States; and suppose that for various reasons the bulbs sold in Canada, manufactured by the subsidiary of the American company, are sold at a very much higher price than those sold by General Electric in the United States: is there anything to prohibit an importer importing into Canada electric bulbs made by the General Electric Company of the United States, the parent of the subsidiary company in Canada to which it has transferred its patent rights?

The answer is very simple.
The patent which covers the territorial jurisdiction of the states of the American union and its territories is one patent; the patent which covers Canada is another patent. You may not, while a patent is in force in Canada, import from abroad that same patented article and bring it into Canada without a licence from the patentee of the Canadian patent. That is so in this and in every other country with the exception, possibly, of Japan; and it is so because we are bound by an international convention which so provides. But the remedy is this. In the first place, if the Canadian company holding the Canadian patent does not adequately supply the market in Canada, then under this act the Canadian patent may be revoked; and in the second place, if the Canadian patentee

Patents of Invention

does manufacture in Canada so as to supply adequately the requirements of the Canadian market and yet charges in Canada an unreasonable price for the manufactured product, then he may be compelled under this bill to reduce his price or to suffer the penalty of having his Canadian patent revoked. These are the remedies which we are now prescribing, and they have no particular reference to the duties imposed upon the import of electric bulbs. I do not know what those duties are. If those duties are too high, I, for one am prepared to consider the question of their reduction on its merits, as I always endeavour to do with respect to the imposition of protective duties for the protection of this market. But I have never, so far as I know, advocated the protection of the Canadian market in cases where I really believed that the Canadian producers were abusing that privilege and taking advantage of this market. I have always held that remedial measures should! be found for that. But, in respect of this bill, I think we are prescribing effective remedial measures. If later this government and this parliament or another government and another parliament desire to place the administration of this act under some special board which is more or less irresponsible to the government and to parliament, that is a matter for parliament to decide; it is a matter with regard to which I now offer no opinion. But that measure for the creation, constitution and organization of a. board may be adopted under legislation separate and distinct from this particular legislation which is now before the house; and the passing of this bill does not in any way prevent parliament in its discretion from enacting legislation which will create and constitute such a board as that suggested.

I will make one further
suggestion. The hon. gentleman said he would be willing to consider the revision of the tariff. That has nothing to do with it. It does not matter what the tariff is, under the act as it is you cannot import these articles, and that is the point. They are using this act as a prohibitive tariff; that is what it amounts to. When I referred to their selling these articles at a price that amounted to an advance of 125 per cent over the duty paid price, I merely meant to indicate the extent to which the abuse of the act had gone. I should like to submit this to the Minister of Justice. Section 65, we are told, adequately deals with this aspect of the matter, but I claim frankly that it does not. Subsection 1,

upon which the Secretary of State has fastened as his argument, reads:
The Attorney General of Canada or any person interested may at any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the grant of a patent apply to the commissioner alleging in the case of that patent that there has been an abuse of the exclusive rights thereunder and asking for relief under this act.
All that does is to provide that the Attorney General of Canada or any other person may apply to the commissioner of patents and say that an abuse has occurred. But there is nothing in the section to say what the commissioner shall do; that has been deleted under the old section 40. I will suggest that we reinstate the major part of subsection (e) of the old section 40. I will move that following subsection 1 of section 65 of this bill there shall be a new subsection, which might be made 1 (a), and which will read:
(la) The commissioner shall then consider the petition and if the parties do not come to an arrangement between themselves, shall proceed to hear and determine the matter, and if it is proved to his satisfaction that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied, or that the patentee has failed to adequately manufacture the patented invention the patentee may be ordered by him to supply the patented article w'ithin reasonable limits at such price as may be fixed by him and in accordance with the custom of the trade to which the invention relates as to the payment and delivery, or to grant licences for the use of the patented invention as may be fixed by him, in either case within and after such time as may be fixed by him and on pain of forfeiture of the payment.
I move that that clause be added to section 65.

In the meantime, while the hon. gentleman is drafting his amendment, I suggest that section 65 should stand until we see the exact terms of the proposed amendment, and as sections 65 and 66 are the ones under discussion and we agreed that those sections might be discussed together, I suggest that we proceed with section 67.

I would like the minister to consider a question which has worried me from time to time in regard to the imposition of these charges. This act is framed for the protection of the public, but

you make the individual who owns the scales pay for the inspection. I do not think that is fair, and I suggest that under this section and at this time consideration should be given to the removal of the charges for inspection of scales. Of course it does not commend itself to me by reason of its antiquity alone, but this practice is followed in every country that has an inspection service; the service takes care of the cost of the operation. That is a principle we have on the statutes in connection with a great many other public services performed by governmental agencies for the protection of the public. The one that occurs to me immediately is in connection with the insurance act. I understand that it is because of the provisions of section 82 that the Department of Justice recommended the amendment which they did, which I have now withdrawn. I have an open mind on the subject, but my first thought was as I have suggested.

The suggestion of my
hon. friend from Hants-iKings (Mr. Ilsley) is that the words "by regulation" in section 82 be struck out. Perhaps the minister will consider that.
Perhaps we had better let that matter stand until we reach it.
Are the regulations changed frequently, or are they not subject to change very often?

I understand that there have not been any changes for three years, so they do not come very often.

Questions

I think when we are dealing with penalties for breach of regulations, if the regulations have been very much the same for many years it is much better to embody the regulations as far as possible in the act itself than to leave them subject to change from time to time and have penalties imposed for a breach of regulations that we know not of.

If I catch the hon. gentleman's idea correctly he suggests that the regulations should be embodied as substantive provisions of the bill. I do not think the department ought to be hampered by having to come to parliament to get regulations to meet the situation when, for instance some new scientific invention comes into general use. If we did not have the power to make regulations the department would be handicapped. I am advised that there have been no changes in the regulations since 1929.
If there have not been many changes, my argument is all the stronger.

Referring to the amendment that the minister proposes to move, it seems to me that $25 is a pretty stiff penalty for a first offence, and that not less than $25 or more than $100 is also very high for a second offence.

That is the maximum. The magistrate does not need to impose $25. The experience of the department is that magistrates are pretty lenient; ten dollars is about the average, and sometimes it is one dollar.
It seems to me that it would be much better to have the penalty definitely set out in the act so that the magistrate would know exactly what to do instead of leaving it to his discretion.
There is a minimum and a maximum penalty.
I think $25 is too high.

It all depends on the offence. It is very difficult to legislate here in advance. We do not know what the contravention of the regulation in question may be. With respect to sections 63 and 64, the short weights and unjust scales sections, the hon. gentleman will observe, if he reads the bill, that very severe penalties are suggested. However, it is very late now to go
into that and I therefore move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.
